title: He Won the World Championship Six Months Ago. In Oslo, He Finished Last.
excerpt: Gukesh Dommaraju's rating has dropped 62 points since his peak. His world ranking has fallen from No. 3 to No. 19. His title defence is months away.
body:
He arrived in Oslo as the youngest world champion in chess history, the teenager from Chennai who dethroned Ding Liren in a nerve-shredding final game just six months ago. He left Norway in last place.

Gukesh Dommaraju scored 8 out of a possible 30 points at the 14th Norway Chess tournament, finishing behind every other competitor in the elite six-player field — behind Magnus Carlsen, behind Vincent Keymer, and behind his compatriot R Praggnanandhaa, who won the event. In the final round, Carlsen beat Gukesh 2-0 in the classical game, completing a clean sweep against the world champion in their head-to-head.

The numbers make for uncomfortable reading. Gukesh's FIDE rating has fallen to 2732, down from a peak of 2794. His world ranking has slipped from No. 3 to No. 19 on the live list. For a reigning world champion preparing to defend his title later this year, the trajectory is alarming.

## A Pattern, Not a Blip

This is not an isolated poor result. Since winning the world championship, Gukesh has struggled to recapture the form that made him the youngest undisputed world champion in history. The burden of the crown — a phenomenon that afflicted his predecessor Ding Liren, who fell out of the world top-20 before losing his title — appears to have transferred.

David Howell, the English grandmaster and commentator, offered blunt advice during the Norway Chess broadcast. "He needs his coaches to tell him to try new things, to switch things up," Howell said. "He's been doing the same thing for the last 18 months. He needs to maybe just play a few games a little safer, play them a little more solid."

Howell went further: "He's taking so much risk every game, even when he's not in form. When you're not in form, that's when to go back to basics. Keep it super simple, take minimum risk."

## The Diaspora's Champion Under Pressure

For millions of Indian chess fans in the diaspora — many of whom stayed up past midnight to watch Gukesh's world championship triumph — this slide is deeply concerning. Chess has become India's quiet export, from Viswanathan Anand's pioneering decades to the current generation of Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa, Arjun Erigaisi, and others. The stakes are high, as Gukesh's performance not only reflects on his personal journey but also on the pride of the Indian community abroad, who have invested emotionally and financially in his success. For many NRIs, Gukesh's ascent mirrors their own aspirations for excellence and recognition on a global stage, making his struggles particularly poignant.

The implications of Gukesh's performance extend beyond the chessboard. A successful title defense could inspire a new generation of chess players in the diaspora, fostering cultural ties and encouraging participation in chess clubs and tournaments across the US, UK, and Canada. Conversely, a lackluster performance could dampen enthusiasm and diminish the support for chess initiatives within these communities. Many diaspora chess enthusiasts have expressed their hopes for Gukesh’s comeback, emphasizing the importance of his success in motivating young players in their local clubs. His journey is often discussed in community forums and at chess academies across the US, UK, and Canada, serving as a powerful narrative for young Indian-origin players.

Gukesh remains the world champion. That title is his until someone takes it from him. But the world championship match, expected later this year, will pit him against a challenger who has earned the right through the Candidates Tournament. If Gukesh enters that match in his current form, the title defense could be short-lived.

Meanwhile, Praggnanandhaa — who finished last after six rounds in the same tournament — reeled off four consecutive wins to claim the Norway Chess title with 18 points. At 20, Praggnanandhaa proved that dramatic reversals of form are possible. The question is whether Gukesh, at 20 himself, can find his own reset before the stakes become existential.

## What Needs to Change

The chess world has seen this before. Carlsen himself endured a rough patch in 2015 before returning stronger. But Carlsen had a decade of world-class experience behind him. Gukesh has six months as world champion and a rating that is trending in the wrong direction.

The prescription is clear, even if the execution is not: play more solidly, take fewer risks in unfavorable positions, and rediscover the accuracy that carried him through the Candidates and the world championship match. A draw, as Howell noted, is a fine result in some games.

Oslo is behind him. What comes next
